chunks.text: Uh, FEC, and we look forward to your submission. We've got you for five minutes, but please leave some time for questions. Will do. So, the Fair Trading Amendment Bill has, in my view, very admirable objectives. Two key objectives as I read the explanatory note are ensuring that the Fair Trading Act is fit for purpose as digital markets evolve, and secondly, enabling efficient and effective enforcement.

And by efficient, I take that to mean cost effective. Effective really means timely. In my view, unfortunately, the Fair Trading Act has become ineffective in relation to digital markets, particularly in the case of overseas online trades, and hugely costly to try and enforce against overseas online traders.

In my written submission, I give the example of Viagogo, the online ticket reseller. And just to give a just very brief overview, Commission wanted to stop some conduct by Viagogo in terms of the way that they were offering tickets for resale.

Brought a case in 2018, wanted an injunction. Viagogo avoided service, said, "You've got to service in Switzerland, go through The Hague convention, do it through diplomatic channels." Argued in the meantime that the High Court didn't have jurisdiction to grant an injunction, actually won that in the High Court.

Court of Appeal had to take that on appeal to the Court of Appeal. Viagogo took all steps to try and resist the proceedings, resisted discovery, sought to delay the proceedings. The Commission said that they took an obstructive attitude. I don't know the rights and wrongs of that, but certainly the High Court made some critical comments.

Continued their defense, despite being penalized for essentially the same conduct in Australia in 2020. So the case took six years, from 2018 to 2024, and then since then it's gone further on appeal. And cases like that are hugely expensive and time-consuming, very hard for the Commerce Commission to run more than one or two cases like that at the same time if they involve that much expense. And in the meantime, you've got ongoing harm to consumers over many years if online traders can't be quickly prevented from engaging in misleading conduct.

Now fortunately, we've got a good model in other legislation for how to deal with this. So the Financial Markets Conduct Act provides a model in relation to how to deal with misleading conduct in financial markets. So the FMA is the regulator for misleading conduct in financial markets, Commerce Commission for everything else, misleading conduct in other markets.

And what you can do under the Financial Markets Conduct Act is the regulator can give notice of a stop order, so the trader has to stop the misleading conduct immediately. They can challenge that order in the courts, but at least the consumer harm is prevented in the meantime. And if the trader doesn't stop the conduct, then the regulator can, as part of the stop order notice, stop the trader from providing services in New Zealand to New Zealand consumers at all. The Financial Markets Authority has exercised its stop order power

to prevent a Dubai corporation from offering securities when the public was misled. I refer to that case, that example, in my written submission. And so that enabled the FMA, in that case, within two months of finding out about the misleading conduct, to stop securities being offered.

So my essential argument is that the Commerce Commission should have the same power to give stop notices as the FMA has. Same sort of situation to stop misleading conduct. And in my view, that's a far more important reform than just increasing the penalties under the act.

Now, I don't have a problem with what's currently proposed in the Amendment Bill. I'm just saying that if you really want to achieve the objectives of the Bill, of ensuring effective and efficient enforcement of the act, and if you really want to achieve the objective in the Bill of ensuring that the Fair Trading Act is fit for purpose as digital markets evolve, then you need these stop order powers more than you need the increased penalties, though I don't mind the increased penalties.

Thanks, John. Thanks. Quick question from me. The stop order power, you're saying FMA already has it. If the Commerce Commission have it, are you saying it would... I'm just making sure we're not duplicating powers. Would it be a separate type for different entities? Yeah. So both the Commerce Commission would have as well as the FMA.

The FMA, of course, only regulate misleading conduct in relation to financial markets, whereas the Commerce Commission regulates misleading conduct everywhere else. Okay. So it's to try and have consistency and ensure that the Commission has the same toolbox. Yeah. Thank you. Your submission's very clear and very comprehensive- Mm... for a person's submission, so I just want to thank you for that, and that'll be duly noted.

Very good. Any other questions from the committee? Unfortunately, we have met time, but- Okay... yeah. No worries. Yeah, that's time. Thanks for coming in. Thank you. Okay. Jayden, are we, or Taryn, are we back to Max, or are we- Uh, we- Is Max here or not? Yeah, we can see him come in. Okay.

And then we have Internet New Zealand. Fantastic. Internet New Zealand, are they in the room? Are they joining via internet? Line is very good. Good morning, Vivian. Sorry, Isabel. Yes. Vivian's here. Good morning. And Isabel. Good morning. We've got you for 10 minutes. We're in your hands.

But it goes quick, so please leave time for questions. Thank you. Okay. Well, thank you for hearing our submission. As you probably know, Internet New Zealand is an independent purpose-driven organization in the community sector, but we're responsible for administering and maintaining the .nz domain name system, the DNS- Mm... on behalf of all New Zealanders.

And a critical part to that is maintaining the .nz registry and the infrastructure that enables .nz websites and email addresses to connect globally. That's sort of a deeply technical process. But we maintain a database of domain name registration data, providing name service to publish the zone file throughout the internet.

We have a subsidiary called the Domain Name Commission. It's an independent subsidiary. They're kind of our regulatory body. And they oversee the .nz domain name market, enforcing the .nz rules, authorize and deauthorize registrars who retail domain names, and investigate complaints, and they operate a dispute resolution service.

So, we are actively involved with our international peers on best practice and response to scams. You can imagine that's a very big issue globally right now, and how best to respond to abusers of the domain name system, usually called DNS abuse.

So, we're a technical expert who provide advice on public policy topics related to the internet and the digital environment. I wanted to just make that introduction because our interest is deep, but relatively small in the context of this whole sub- the whole area that you're considering.

And I wanted to hand over to Isabel, who'll talk through the specific feedback in relationship to this bill. Thanks, Isabel. Thank you. I'm going to introduce the two organizations, InternetNZ, the registry, and the Domain Name Commission, so people can understand the nature of the tools that we have because we have got a request for a- Great... clarification of the definition.

So that's why I'm just explaining a bit more about the powers. InternetNZ, through the operation of the.nz registry, actually has the technical ability to disrupt scams at the domain name system level, and that is through disabling a domain name by putting it on a hold or suspending it.

When that happens, the entire domain name is taken down. We can't carve out specific offending content or take down... We can only take down the whole service that's enabled by that domain name. So that's the work technically that InternetNZ can do at the .nz registry level.

How it's actually enabled is that the Domain Name Commission plays that oversight role, and they are the entity that can take the decision to suspend or cancel a domain name. I'm going to move into the clarification that we're seeking. But I just want to reconfirm that due to the shifts in the industry, the domain name system internationally is looking at disrupting, particularly phishing and malware, and the Domain Name Commission is looking into its role, how it can better respond to technical abuse.

So, the clarification that we're seeking is that we propose a new definition that better describes the type of services included in the current wording, which is internet domain name registration service. Those words, "internet domain name registration service," would normally mean the registrar that retails to the public, when in fact it's actually central top-level domain name sys- um, operators, like InternetNZ, who runs the top of .nz. So they have the full

oversight across the whole space. We're saying that it's much more effective if a registry is also able to have the benefits of the safe harbor, and at the moment, it's not clear that we're included. So I'm not going to read out the whole basis of our written submission, but we have proposed wording there. We say that the policy intent is better achieved if it's clarified that both the wholesalers and retailers of domain names are covered by the safe harbor.

And we are in an environment where organizations like the Domain Name Commission and other threat providers are also doing scam prevention. So we want to extend- The definition of registration services to those providing oversight and compliance services.

So I hope that nuance can be adapted and that will better provide for the intent of the legislation, the policy intent, so that all of the key parties can actually obtain that safe harbor. Thank you. Thank you. We've got a question from Todd Stevens.

Oh, no, mine was just a comment to say thanks for your submission. Yeah, we'll definitely take that on board. And you've outlined your case pretty clearly, so thank you. So just the other key point we wanted to make relates to the trusted flagger network set out the accompanying regulatory impact statement as a non-legislative option that's currently being scoped.

We recommend the trusted flagger network could be given greater status and legislated. Giving the trusted flagger network a statutory mandate would provide entities acting in scam disruption, including the Domain Name Commission, the assurance that the actions are proportionate and meet the legal threshold for safe harbor.

So I think that was the second key point we wanted to bring to your attention. Very good. Okay. Thank you very much for your presentation, Vivian and Isabel. We have met time, but, appreciate that. We'll feed into our select committee process. Okay. Thank you. Thank you. Have we got Kari Quince?
Just joining.
Kia ora, Kari. Are you there?

Kia ora. Can you hear me? Yes, we can. We've only got you for five minutes. You've got a pretty comprehensive three pages. Can I just encourage you to just focus on your top two or three points? Because time will go very fast. That's okay. Yeah. Can you still hear me? Yes. Okay, sweet. Okay.

I'm not fully against this bill or anything. I agree with stopping big multinationals from treating fines as a cost of doing business, giving the Commerce Commission a faster enforcement tool, fighting online scams and updating product safety standards faster.

But I have a few worries. I'm worried about the overwhelming volume of legislation being rushed through Parliament. When laws move at this pace, frequently strip back treaty protections, it creates deep anxiety across our community. Compared to major constitutional changes, a consumer bill might not look like the primary concern, but when Parliament moves in haste, officials neglect critical mechanisms buried in the fine print.

So why would citizens not scrutinize every detail? Under the banner of consumer protection, this bill shifts enforcement from a criminal regime requiring proof beyond reasonable doubt with $600,000 fine caps to a civil regime with a lower balance of probabilities standard and penalties up to $5 million. This expansion comes right off the back of a recent public sector budget cut to the Commerce Commission. Will

the Commission actually have the resources needed to manage this massive increase in litigation capacity, or will enforcement simply fail to private competitors filing costly civil lawsuits? In primary industries like farming and fishing, minor operational slips like an uncalibrated scale on a boat or a packing typo on produce become easy targets. As the Insurance Council of New Zealand highlighted, standard statutory liability insurance does not cover

civil pecuniary penalties. While multinationals absorb civil litigation out of global reserves, local Kiwi operators and Māori enterprises face an uninsurable liability gap. How can we justify exposing local operators to sudden liquidation over an honest operational mistake?

The most severe oversight, however, is how the regime interacts with Whenua Māori. While Section 342 of Te Tiriti Whenua Māori Act protects land titles from direct execution, this bill creates an indirect economic backdoor. A multimillion-dollar penalty forced onto a trading arm triggers corporate insolvency. The High Court liquidator can seize fishing quota, livestock, and machinery, or lease out the Whenua to third

parties to pay court debts. What is the value of protecting land titles on paper if the commercial engine funding Whenua housing, environmental care, and local jobs is wiped out underneath it? I urge the committee to- Direct officials to engage directly with Te Puni Kōkiri to assess these indirect commercial impacts to include and express savings or safe harbor provision protecting existing rights under Te Ture Whenua Māori Act and Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

Tena koutou. Thank you, Kari, for your submission. Are there any questions from members? No. No. Thank you. I think your points were pretty clear, and you certainly put a lot of information in your submission, so thank you for engaging in the process. Thank you. We've got FINCAP in the room. Welcome.

You must be Jake. Yeah. Apologies from Fleur, was on leave when we got the call for this, so- No problem. We've got you for 10 minutes, but yeah, obviously if you have a bit of time for questions, it can be quite helpful. Awesome. Thank you. So if you're unfamiliar, I know many here have worked with financial mentors and us before. Thank you for your time working with us.

But FINCAP, we are out there as an umbrella organization across currently around 183 services who support financial mentors in their communities around the country. There's over 700 financial mentors out there. I'm here with you today because I often get calls from financial mentors or emails from financial mentors saying, "I just can't believe this unacceptable thing from a debt collector continues to happen, and I can't really find a way through it."

And it really aligns with the objectives of this bill, focusing on it in the written submission. Also highlight we've got our Voices report out tomorrow. In that, we've seen 121% increase in debt in our system over the last five years. We're almost at a billion dollars of debt in all sorts of different forms, and some of those, although quite small, can cause a lot of problems in people's lives as debt collectors pursue them.

60% of mentors encounter clients experiencing issues with debt collectors often or very often, 34% sometimes. So it's pretty universal out there for the financial mentors. 86% had seen debt collectors make demands for repayment that prevented clients from affording food or other essentials, and two-thirds had seen excessively frequent contact from debt collectors, which is unconstructive really when you look at someone being unable to pay.

So we do think that debt collection is a legitimate part of our economy, but the rules around it need tidying up to stop needlessly harmful contact that doesn't benefit anyone. I've been working on this for coming up six years. I know there was a good look at this as well in the review that led to the introduction to high-cost lending protections, but we constantly get these reasons why work stalls in this space, and I'm really asking you to seize the moment and the objectives of this bill to do something in this space.

The cost of living keeps biting people, and we need better law to prevent harassment and coercion in years to come from debt collectors where people have gotten into debt that they can't handle and didn't anticipate they weren't going to be able to handle. FINCAP and financial mentors were glad to work with Minister Bailey through the Consumer Protection Partnership Forum, setting up a group with officials and getting into this a bit. That led to some good work and some good discussion. In the targeted consultation for this, there was a good look at

harassment and coercion, but the timelines for this piece of work that led to this bill meant it ended up being much narrower than the few things that were put in front of people. Again, we're stalled. It leaves households constantly exposed, and really that exposure in terms of harassment and coercion, which I'm focusing on, is that we don't see a good case to take complaints to the Commerce Commission about these problems because the Commerce Commission is left without a penalty for these two things.

So it's not economic for them to go to the court and get an order in one instance saying, "Hey, you shouldn't do that." The debt collector then says, "Or else what?" There might be something, although it's a high bar, around getting some money back to a person where it's been taken in circumstances where it shouldn't. But again, is it really a good deterrent?

It doesn't make sense for the Commerce Commission to put resources into it unless they're backed with a penalty in those circumstances. And yeah, as I said, financial mentors aren't taking those cases as often as they would because they know there's a bit of a dead end there. When I talk about coercion, I'm talking about debt collectors saying they won't leave your house until you agree to their demand or the minimum demand.

Debt collectors yelling abuse down the phone at a financial mentor who's just asking for proof of a debt that they claim someone owes. And we get a taste of financial mentor, financial mentors see a bit of the harassment too. Not all of it. You sort of get different reactions once a financial mentor gets involved, but occasionally some of those systems are so sloppy at debt collectors that we see financial mentors' numbers associated with a file, and that gets put onto the computer.

They get automatically dialed, automatic messages, texts, emails, and then sometimes you try and call back and ask, "Hey, I've had this contact," and the contact center you go back to is so hard to navigate. You can't actually respond to the request for contact, which is a bit ridiculous. We also get situations where an agreement is made after contact is made, but then the automatic calls, automatic dialing doesn't stop because someone doesn't know how to stop it in the system at the debt collector.

It has real consequences. People just stop answering contact in general. It means we see drop-off from financial mentors trying to support someone, because if someone doesn't recognize the number, they don't pick up their phone. They're changing email addresses and phone numbers because it's just so impractical to live when they're getting constant demands to pay something that they've clearly stated or given evidence that they can't pay.

Sometimes as well, the harassment will wear people down and they'll give away their rent money, their food money, power money. The consequences of that hardship will intensify and they're just back in the cycle. It leads to more hospitalizations, strain in relationships with those partners, family, and friends that they lean on at times as they try and get this problem sorted.

And also that sobering research we've put in a written submission around suicidal ideation. Again, that's in the written submission. Also put forward in our submission that there needs to be a lot more guidance in the space and perhaps across a range of regulators. It was mentioned before of sort of the crossover that happens in terms of what the law says with the financial markets and also the broader markets.

ACCC guidelines in Australia are pretty good. They're much clearer about where the line is. It would help us when we're negotiating with debt collectors. It would help them too in terms of what's expected, and it would mean less having to go to the Commerce Commission and go through all the processes there that are very costly and timely, time-consuming. And also stressing we really support the penalties going up, although we make the point in our submission that you should look at the Australian penalties too. We do speak with some complaints, people at Australian

businesses at times, and they sort of comment that, "Hey, we see less complaints from New Zealand and a bit different regulator there too," so don't want to be a soft target or maybe not having as much attention on compliance here as there is in Australia.

Lastly, I just wanted to touch on, there's been reasons put down for delaying this work on applying penalties to coercion and harassment in briefings from officials that have been released. There is some piece of work that needs to be done around the definition of harassment, it seems. That's all good, but it's nothing that can't be worked through if it's prioritized.

And to my understanding, a good piece of work or review of the Fair Trading Act as a whole is long overdue. Mm-hmm. These things do need to be prioritized. So many households are struggling with cost of living pressures right now that will have a long tail. And it should also be noted from reading that advice, I didn't spot anything in there that really justified not getting on with penalties for coercion.

There was talk about harassment, but there's no reason you can't go for coercion now. So, putting it there as something the committee might be able to recommend. Thank you for your time. Thanks, Jake. Elena. We're... I'm hoping to get y- this will be your only submission, so we will receive advice back on this about what the gap in the law is. There's unconscionable conduct at one end, there's unfair terms, but you're talking about conduct outside of a transaction, but over the course of the price that a transaction would cost a consumer.

So are you looking for regulation around, like is it a regulatory making power that sets out kind of what coercion would be acceptable? What sort of manipulation is just normal commercial practice, or are you looking for a blanket ban and then enforcement at the concom level?

Yeah, I guess a blanket ban technically exists right now- Yeah... in that as it's written, it's a penalty for that which then gives the regulator a bit more space for guidance to say- Yeah... this is what's expected and then can adapt that as inevitably markets will change. Do you think ACCC style fines for conduct that can be levied at the regulator level or do you think it's court process fines?

Looking at Australia, it seems like they've got the whole menu and they adapt to the circumstances. I know this was largely talked around supermarkets and those two geographies have very different structures, so it might be different depending on who's done what. So the more the better is probably our position there in terms of infringements if those are going to be most useful to deter through to criminal.

We'll seek advice on this, and I anticipate that we will be told that the formulation of the law as it is now will dampen this kind of conduct in the market. Do you think the law as it's formulated now will do enough? Not really, no. No. I think just when a debt collector is at someone's house or they're getting trained, it's not getting through to that point and I don't think a change in penalty's going to change that at the moment.

Yeah. Thank you. Just a supplementary on the back of that. Do you think there's a bit of space for, you used the word harmonization in your submission between Australia's processes and ours? Yeah. There is a study that was done sort of working with us, and it looked at the definition adopting undue, which brings over a bit of case law from Australia, and that has some good definition.

Harassment is an interesting concept here. It is legitimate to follow up with someone and say, "We assert you owe this. You need to get back to us. Here's how to get back to us." Undue goes to another level where you're well aware of the circumstances. Yeah. And you can constantly keep going. Hey, thanks so much for your submission and the work you and your team do.

It's fantastic. Thank you. Thanks all. We now have the Community Law Centres Aotearoa. Karen. Mm. Welcome. Tena koutou, Mr. Chair and members of the committee. I almost want to say, yeah, what he said in some ways. Ko Karen Hodgson tēnei. I'm pleased to be here for Community Law Centres Aotearoa.

Some of you we've worked with, and I've been in hui with, but if you don't know, we are the national body for the 24 Community Law Centres across the country. We provide free legal advice across an incredibly broad range of legal issues, and free legal advice across a broad range of issues for people who can't afford a lawyer. So, we provide consumer advice across the board, including on the Fair Trading Act- And making Commerce Commission complaints.

Just some of the examples of things we work on, we get complaints about online sales and drip pricing, so people coming in with the full price not really disclosed to them when they're buying online. Parking fines, and parking companies effectively stonewalling people when they are trying to appeal, no evidence being provided, and potentially misleading or coercive debt collection practices asserting money's owed when maybe it's a money claim in and of itself and there's no evidence, and overstated debt collection fees, for example, like a percentage, a blanket

percentage on top of a debt. You've heard from FINCAP just now on some of these issues, and I agree wholeheartedly, and we see very similar issues across community law centers. We generally support this bill and the changes in it. Our written submissions, as you know, focused on the change to the act to make it a predominantly civil regime, with higher penalties, rather than a criminal regime. The regulatory impact statement sets out really well stakeholder views. I think we're in there, and the Commerce Commission concerns

about the effectiveness of the current regime and that it would be an easier road to enforce under a civil liability regime. I just want to also take the opportunity to raise that we, along with FINCAP and others, are advocating for the establishment of a financial rights legal service. We're seeing so many really tricky and unregulated debt collection practices, but also other kinds of financial rights issues that need specialized financial advice, which currently financial mentors have some access to community law centers, but

community law centers also need this specialized advice as well. So I'm just putting that out there if anybody's interested in knowing more. We did raise this in relation to the financial services reform bills as well. And we invite members to work with us on that. So just in connection with this, and going back to debt collection, as you know, Section 23 doesn't have any penalties associated with it.

It's not within the bill at the moment, but it's squarely within the objectives of the bill, to strengthen deterrence and compliance and greater enforcement and greater effective and efficient enforcement. We frequently see debt collection agencies ignoring people when they dispute a debt, not providing evidence behind a debt, people feeling coerced into paying, basically worn down because it's too hard to complain or too hard to resolve the issue.

And sometimes these can have really quite significant impacts. Jake's talked about people going without food or what they need to do, essentials, in order to make these payments. But also it can end up on a credit report. We're seeing people who are ending up in civil proceedings, and attachment orders for debt that they barely even knew about or haven't really had a chance to argue about.

So we've agreed with MBIE and its consultation paper that Tier 1 penalties should apply. We do think there should be a criminal response available because of the nature of some of this behavior can be at that end, and given that it includes physical force and that interpersonal nature of the behavior when it relates to door knocking, approaches in person, that sort of thing. We think that work should be progressed on this front, and that this is an opportunity to really respond to this harm that's occurring in our communities to some of the most vulnerable people.

And we understand that time was an issue, and we really want to push back on that and say this is incredibly important work, and we'd really like to see it progressed. Those are really all my remarks, and I'm just open for any questions. Thank you. We've got first questions from Arinna Williams. Thank you. Really appreciate your submission. And I am interested in other parts of it, but I just want to clarify, do you support FINCAP's submission, particularly on coercion in a provision to prevent as a blanket ban and then with associated fines?

Coercion on its own? Yeah. I think we haven't gone down too much thinking on that one. I think there's a way of working it out so that you can have harassment and coercion. Okay. Not opposed to it. But I'd like to see the work done on maybe working it out so that it is harassment and coercion, but I definitely see merit in that. We just haven't gone- And as well for harassment, you think if they were together that would be the appropriate way to make that- I think if you can-- There is a civil and criminal regime in

the Harassment Act, or there was. And we could sort of see something similar along those lines although, yeah, that would need some working through. But not against that at all. Just wonder if there's a way, whether there's some useful Australian case law on harassment and coercion that could be brought over as well.

Yeah, probably just need some, that we'd need to think a bit more about that. Can you come back to me on a different query? Yeah. Dr. David Wilson. I see one of your recommendations is the licensing of debt collection agencies- Mm... and that that should be run by the FMA. Mm-hmm. How hard? And I have a supplementary question.

How hard would that be? How hard would it be? They're already licensing a bunch of other entities and agencies, so it would be part of that process, I imagine. I think the things that we're recommending there are part of a package, and I think you'd need some additional guidance for debt collection agencies and along the lines of the Australian guidance, to really make that work And related to that, you were recommending some kind of organization around financial rights and- Mm-hmm... and then, if you like, how that's resolved, the resolution of that. Where would that sit?

Our previous proposal has been for that to sit in as a unit of community law centers. We currently have other specialized centers. Yeah. And it could be a specialized community law center, much like in Melbourne or other parts of Australia. And we really see that penalties undertakings are a really great and appropriate way to fund that service.

Thank you. We're working at a policy level on that. Just- Mm-hmm... wanted to ask you about the way, like enforcement in your observations, having acted for clients on either the resources that are available to ComCom to take on some of the bigger issues or are we designing a system which isn't addressing the right end of the market? Would be my first question.

And then interested in, you brought up sort of hidden fees, drip pricing. Do you think as well that we've designed a system which is meant to hit the top end of town with bigger penalties, but what you're describing will always by nature be one consumer who's paid $30 when they intended to pay 10?

Mm-hmm. Um. Just on your first question, yeah, we do find, the Commerce Commission has limited resources, and the Commerce Commission has said this would make it easier. But yeah, the question remains, I mean, I'm not really, I think our observation is that they don't necessarily have the tool, not the tools, the resources available to be able to actually carry out enforcement in this way.

But it's sometimes more about, and I think they've said it themselves, it's actually about the teeth, not so much the resources. What would make it easier for community law to take some of those consumer cases, particularly around the coercion, harassment kind of conduct issues rather than they, with, "I've got a consumer here who's paying more than they intended to pay through use of sort of discriminatory pricing techniques"?

How, what would make it easier for us to? Yeah. Like if you were designing a system where community law was taking a bunch of cases and they were sort of consumer cases and you're going to the courts or using dispute tribunal- Yeah... whatever that was to do that, what would that look like? Well, we're doing that now really in terms of making complaints and then raising these kinds of issues at the disputes tribunal.

Mm-hmm. Harassment and coercion, you can't do that. But misleading, deceptive, that kind of thing we're raising in the disputes tribunal, yeah, as those kind of arguments. Yeah. Yeah. As to your, the point about... I think some of that drip pricing stuff, that does affect a lot of consumers. I wouldn't say necessarily that it just affects, the drip pricing just affects one person, that it's the way that the process works online for multiple consumers to buy in that way.

And that you sign up for this, but next thing you know you've actually signed up for three years of a subscription to something or add-ons to things that you didn't really know you were signing up to. So it affects more than the one. Yeah. What would it take for community law to be running a class action around those issues? Hmm. Yeah. Hmm. Yeah, that's a really good question.

Resources, those cases are really intensive and we have a lot of pro bono support through Te Ara Ture, and we're actually doing some litigation work and intervening in cases now. Te Ara Ture is our pro bono clearing house. But they're so resource intensive. You have to think about even when we're doing family law and sort of straying a bit, but you can either represent people and spend that time doing that, and that's really time and resource intensive, or helping multiple people. So it really is a balancing of our resource.

Hmm. I mean, that's open to us to do. It's a resource question. Yeah. Thanks, Karen, for your submission today and appreciate the work you're doing as well. Thank you. Thank you. Members, we actually have Tony Gavaghan. Are you happy to present now a little bit ahead of schedule? We might hear from you, and then we'll have just a short break.
If that's all right.

So we've got Tony and Marcus. That's right. On behalf of Fort Stafford Limited. Thank you. We've got you for 10 minutes, gentlemen, but please leave some time for questions at the end of that if you'd like. Good morning. I'm Marcus Ganley from Franks Ogilvie. We're on as special counsel. I'm here with Tony Gavaghan, and we're appearing on behalf of Port Stafford and JFL.

Our submission is really focused on our client's practical experience in dealing with a major fair trade issue centered on a breach of one of the fundamental provisions of the act. Section 9 of the FTA deals with misleading and deceptive conduct. Our submission is inspired by the experience of the Feltex litigants represented by Mr. Gavaghan on behalf of Fort Stafford and JFL who lost significant sums following what the Supreme Court found to be a breach of Section 9 of the Fair Trading Act.

Despite the Supreme Court finding statements in the Feltex share prospectus breached Section 9 of the FTA, there has been no remedy for investors. Among the objectives of the bill in front of this committee are to strengthen deterrence of unfair trading conduct and to support appropriate consequences for breaches.
